name: Join.cloud

hlido_opinion.headline: Zero-config rooms where AI agents collaborate in real time — MCP- and A2A-native, every room a git repo, priced pay-as-you-go over x402 — a clean piece of agent-to-agent infrastructure.
hlido_opinion.body: Join.cloud is a well-executed answer to a concrete multi-agent need: shared rooms where agents from different tools and machines exchange messages, share files and coordinate tasks with no infrastructure to manage. The design decisions are strong and agent-first: rooms are created by name with no API keys or registration ('tell your agent to connect and join the welcome room'), it's first-class on both MCP and Google's A2A protocol (with copy-paste setup for Claude Code/Cursor/Windsurf and a raw A2A curl example), and every room is a git repo so agents push code/configs/artifacts and you can clone from anywhere. The use-case framing is unusually credible — researcher/writer/reviewer loops, coder/tester CI loops, cross-machine collaboration, ops monitoring — each shown as a realistic transcript rather than vague promise. Pricing is transparent and genuinely novel: Free through Enterprise ($0–$29.99/mo) paid via the x402 protocol (USDC on Base, no accounts or cards), and the server is fully open-source for self-hosting. The honest limits: it's young infrastructure, and reliability, delivery guarantees, security isolation between rooms, and how well the git-backed rooms scale are exactly what a landing page can't prove. For builders wiring up multi-agent, cross-tool or cross-machine workflows, it's one of the more thoughtfully designed agent-collaboration surfaces around.

tier_rationale: STEADY (74) for a clean, genuinely agent-native collaboration layer: zero-config named rooms, first-class MCP + A2A support, git-backed rooms, transparent x402 pricing and an open-source self-host path, with credible, specific use-case transcripts. Not higher because it's young infrastructure whose reliability, delivery guarantees, cross-room security isolation and scale are unverifiable from the surface. Not FADING because the design, protocol support and self-hostable openness are substantial and well thought through.
what_it_does_well: Zero-config: create a room by name, no API keys/registration — an agent connects in one command
First-class MCP and Google A2A protocol support, with copy-paste setup for Claude Code/Cursor/Windsurf and a raw A2A curl example
Every room is a git repo — agents push code/configs/artifacts, clone from anywhere
Credible, specific use-case transcripts (researcher/writer/reviewer, coder/tester CI loop, cross-machine, ops monitoring)
Transparent pricing (Free–$29.99/mo) via x402 (USDC on Base, no accounts/cards) and a fully open-source, self-hostable server
what_it_fails_at: Young infrastructure: reliability, uptime and delivery guarantees are unproven on the surface
Security isolation between rooms and access-control model aren't detailed on the landing page
Git-backed-room scaling and history/storage limits (100 msg free tier) may constrain heavier use
x402/USDC-on-Base payment is novel but niche — may be unfamiliar friction for some buyers
best_for: Developers wiring up multi-agent workflows where agents from different tools/machines must coordinate
Teams wanting a git-backed shared workspace agents can push artifacts to and humans can clone
Builders who value MCP + A2A protocol-native, zero-config, self-hostable collaboration
not_recommended_for: Production workloads needing proven reliability, delivery guarantees and documented security isolation today
Organisations that can't use x402/USDC payments or need traditional invoicing at higher tiers
Simple single-agent tasks where a shared collaboration room adds no value
red_flags: Reliability, delivery guarantees and cross-room security isolation are the properties that make shared-room infra safe, and none are evidenced on the surface — validate before trusting it with sensitive multi-agent work.
Payment is via the x402 protocol (USDC on Base) with no accounts/cards — verify it fits your procurement and compliance needs.
